blueprint.title: Release Artifact Reconciliation Engine
blueprint.scenario: A small in-house build platform tracks every software release artifact—binaries, checksums, manifests—across three stages: staging, QA sign-off, and production promotion. A finance-ops engineer must reconcile per-artifact cost allocations: each artifact billed to a cost center must match the cost center recorded on the artifact's original build record, and promoted artifacts must carry the correct promotion chain from staging through QA to production with no gaps. The codebase is ~1,200 lines across a Python ingestion layer, a SQLite schema manager, and a SQL query engine that produces the final reconciliation report.
blueprint.instruction_draft:
You maintain the release artifact reconciliation tool at `/app/reconciler/`. Running `python reconcile.py --report` produces a CSV report at `/app/output/report.csv` with one row per artifact: columns `artifact_id`, `cost_center`, `billed_center`, `promotion_chain`, `reconciled` (boolean). A reconciliation is correct when: (1) `reconciled` is TRUE only when `cost_center` equals `billed_center` AND the `promotion_chain` column contains the complete ordered sequence `staging->qa->production` for every promoted artifact; (2) artifacts that were never promoted to production must be absent from the report; (3) each artifact appears exactly once regardless of how many billing events exist for it—the billed center is the one from the most recent billing event for that artifact; (4) promotion chain completeness is checked by traversal order, so a chain that jumps from staging directly to production without a recorded QA step must not be marked complete.

Sample runs on the bundled test fixture produce a report, but the tool is silently wrong on certain inputs. Find and fix all defects so that `python reconcile.py --report` produces a correct CSV on both the bundled fixture and any inputs generated by the verifier. Your fix must survive inputs that include artifacts billed multiple times, artifacts with out-of-order promotion event timestamps, artifacts promoted in non-standard stage sequences, and cost-center strings that differ only in case.
requirements: `reconciled` is TRUE only when cost_center equals billed_center (case-insensitive comparison) AND promotion_chain is exactly 'staging->qa->production'
artifacts never promoted to production are absent from the report
each artifact appears exactly once; billed_center comes from the most-recent billing event by event timestamp
promotion chain is validated by actual traversal order of stage transitions, not by presence of stage names; a staging->production skip fails the chain check
environment: Dockerfile FROM python:3.13-slim-bookworm, installs only stdlib (sqlite3 built-in)
/app/reconciler/reconcile.py: CLI entry point (~120 lines), calls ingest and report modules

/app/reconciler/ingest.py: reads CSV fixtures from /app/data/, populates SQLite at /app/reconciler/db.sqlite (~200 lines); contains bug A: most-recent billing event selection uses MAX(amount) instead of MAX(event_ts), so for artifacts billed twice the wrong billed_center is chosen when the larger-amount event is not the most recent

/app/reconciler/report.py: executes SQL query to produce the reconciliation CSV (~180 lines); contains bug B: the promotion chain completeness check is done with a SQL LIKE '%staging%' AND LIKE '%qa%' AND LIKE '%production%' pattern match rather than ordering-aware traversal, so a chain of 'staging->production->qa' passes when it should not; this bug is only observable by running the tool against data that has out-of-order chains, not from reading the query alone because the logic looks plausible at a glance

/app/reconciler/schema.py: SQLite schema DDL and migration logic (~150 lines); has a subtle schema issue: the promotions table stores stage transitions but the index on (artifact_id, stage_to) is non-unique, causing the traversal query used in the fixed code to need a DISTINCT or GROUP BY to avoid phantom duplicate chain segments — this interacts with bug B so fixing only the LIKE pattern does not fully solve the chain check on multiply-promoted artifacts
/app/reconciler/utils.py: shared helpers, string normalization (~80 lines); cost-center normalization function exists but is not called in the billing join in report.py

/app/data/artifacts.csv, billings.csv, promotions.csv: bundled fixture with ~40 artifacts, designed so the sample report looks plausible (reconciled counts seem reasonable), but does not expose the billing-recency bug or the chain-ordering bug because the fixture happens to have ascending amounts correlating with recency and no out-of-order chains
/app/output/ directory: created at runtime by reconcile.py

Verifier generates fresh fixtures with: artifacts billed multiple times where larger amount is the older event; promotion chains with stage order shuffled (staging->production->qa); artifacts with cost centers differing only in uppercase; artifacts with exactly two complete forward chains to test deduplication; these are written to /app/data/ before calling python reconcile.py --report and then the CSV is parsed and checked
blueprint.internal_hint: Difficulty comes from two interacting data-dependent bugs that are not visible by reading. Bug A (ingest.py): billing event selection uses MAX(amount) not MAX(event_ts), so the wrong billed_center is chosen when the most-recent event has a smaller amount—only visible by running on data where amounts are not monotone with time. Bug B (report.py + schema.py interaction): the chain completeness check uses LIKE substring matching instead of ordered traversal; on the fixture this passes accidentally because no fixture row has an out-of-order chain. Fixing only bug B still fails because the non-unique index on promotions produces duplicate intermediate rows that the fixed traversal query double-counts unless a DISTINCT or GROUP BY is added—this is the second cause interaction. Additionally, the cost-center comparison in the reconciled flag computation calls utils.normalize() only on cost_center but not on billed_center, so case differences are not caught. The agent must: (1) run the tool against crafted or generated data and observe wrong output, (2) trace ingest.py to find the MAX(amount) error, (3) trace report.py to find the LIKE-based chain check, (4) inspect schema.py to find the non-unique index causing phantoms, and (5) notice the asymmetric normalization call. The fixture data deliberately makes the tool appear correct, so the agent cannot rely on sample output to validate fixes.
blueprint.trap: An agent that reads ingest.py and spots the MAX(amount) bug, fixes it, then reads report.py and replaces the LIKE check with an ordering-aware check, will still fail the hidden tests because the non-unique promotions index produces duplicate stage transition rows that the new traversal query counts twice, making chains appear longer than they are. The interaction only manifests on inputs with re-inserted or duplicated promotion events, which the fixture does not include. A shallow verifier that only runs the provided fixture will incorrectly conclude the fix is complete.
tests: Verifier writes a billings fixture where artifact A1 has two billing events: older event (higher amount) to cost center 'INFRA', newer event (lower amount) to 'PLATFORM'; build record says cost center is 'PLATFORM'; checks that billed_center in report is 'PLATFORM' and reconciled is TRUE
Verifier writes a promotions fixture where artifact A2 has transitions: staging->production (skipping QA); checks that A2.promotion_chain is NOT 'staging->qa->production' and reconciled is FALSE

Verifier writes a promotions fixture where artifact A3 has duplicate promotion rows (same artifact_id, same stage transition appears twice due to re-runs); checks that A3 appears exactly once and chain is evaluated correctly without double-counting
Verifier writes artifacts where cost_center is 'Finance' and billed_center billing event has 'FINANCE' (uppercase); checks that reconciled is TRUE (case-insensitive match)
Verifier writes artifacts that were billed but never promoted to production; checks these artifact_ids are absent from report.csv
Verifier checks that the report CSV has no duplicate artifact_id rows across all test fixtures combined
Accuracy threshold: at least 95% of artifact rows in the hidden fixture must have the correct reconciled value (TRUE or FALSE) — this requires all four bugs to be fixed, not just one or two

verifier_knob.name: accuracy_threshold
verifier_knob.effect: Raising to 1.0 requires every single edge case to be handled perfectly; lowering to 0.80 allows a partial fix (e.g., fixing only the billing-recency bug) to pass, making the task easier

expected_failure_modes: Agent reads ingest.py, fixes MAX(amount)->MAX(event_ts), runs sample fixture which now produces same-looking output, declares done without checking chain logic
Agent fixes the LIKE chain check to use ordering but does not notice the non-unique index phantom rows, causing the fixed traversal to still misclassify multiply-promoted artifacts
Agent fixes billing recency and chain ordering but misses the asymmetric case-normalization, failing cost-center case tests
Agent constructs a test case manually that happens not to exercise the promotions deduplication issue and concludes the fix is complete

Agent patches report.py with a Python-side chain validator rather than fixing the SQL, gets most cases right but misses artifacts with duplicate promotion rows because the Python code still receives duplicate rows from the query

speedrun: cat /app/reconciler/ingest.py  # find MAX(amount) bug in billing recency query
cat /app/reconciler/report.py  # find LIKE-based chain check and asymmetric normalize() call
cat /app/reconciler/schema.py  # find non-unique index on promotions(artifact_id, stage_to)
cat /app/reconciler/utils.py   # confirm normalize() exists and its signature
# Edit ingest.py: replace MAX(amount) with MAX(event_ts) in billing event subquery
# Edit report.py: replace LIKE '%staging%' AND LIKE '%qa%' AND LIKE '%production%' with ordered traversal using window function or CTE that checks stage sequence staging->qa->production in order
# Edit report.py: add DISTINCT or GROUP BY artifact_id,stage_from,stage_to to promotions subquery to eliminate phantom duplicate rows from non-unique index
# Edit report.py: wrap billed_center with normalize() (or LOWER()) in the reconciled = (cost_center = billed_center) comparison, mirroring existing normalize() call on cost_center
python reconcile.py --report && cat /app/output/report.csv  # verify fixes on bundled fixture
# Manually craft edge-case CSV: artifact with two billing events (older=higher amount), write to /app/data/, run report, check billed_center is from newer event
# Craft promotion fixture with staging->production skip, verify reconciled=FALSE
# Craft artifact with cost_center='Finance', billed as 'FINANCE', verify reconciled=TRUE
invalid_failure_risks: All four bugs are explicitly documented with file locations and exact symptoms in the blueprint, making them statically visible by source reading — the claimed 'not visible by reading' property is false, undermining the difficulty model entirely
The 'trap' (non-unique index phantom rows) is also visible by reading schema.py and understanding the fixed traversal query, so it provides no additional genuine difficulty over static analysis
If the verifier's generated fixtures don't precisely hit the MAX(amount) edge case boundary (e.g., if event_ts ties are possible), test results could be ambiguous

The SQL ordered traversal fix has multiple valid implementations (recursive CTE, window functions, aggregation); if the verifier checks for a specific SQL pattern rather than output correctness, valid fixes could be rejected
The 95% accuracy threshold means an agent could pass with only 3 of 4 bugs fixed if the fixture distribution happens to not heavily weight the missed bug — hollow partial solution might pass
review.reasons: Genuine difficulty scores 2 because all four bugs are statically visible by reading the documented source files — the blueprint explicitly names the bug location, variable, and symptom for each defect, so a systematic agent reading 5 files solves the task in ~15 commands without needing crafted inputs or dynamic exploration. The claimed 'not visible by reading' and 'only observable by running' properties in the blueprint are contradicted by the blueprint itself disclosing every bug completely. Additionally, the 95% accuracy threshold risks a partial-fix solution passing if the hidden fixture distribution is skewed.
fixes: Make bugs emergent rather than planted: instead of documenting 'ingest.py contains bug A: MAX(amount)...', write the actual buggy code without labeling it as a bug — let the agent discover it by running tests and tracing failures, not by reading a bug map

Use a single bundled fixture that appears correct on the surface (as stated) but add a verifier fixture that the agent cannot see at task time — remove all hints about which files contain bugs from the instruction; the instruction should only describe the desired behavior, not the bug locations

Raise the accuracy threshold to 100% (or >=98%) to eliminate the risk that fixing 3 of 4 bugs passes; alternatively add explicit per-test-case pass/fail checks rather than a single aggregate threshold so partial fixes cannot squeak through

To preserve the interacting-bug difficulty, obfuscate the interaction: e.g., make the non-unique index issue appear only when a separate data migration script is run (which the agent must also discover and invoke), so fixing report.py alone is insufficient and the interaction isn't apparent from static reading of schema.py

verdicts.reason: Cell suppression is a statistical disclosure control problem, entirely different from artifact promotion chain validation and cost center reconciliation.
Setting up an MLflow tracking server is a DevOps/infrastructure task with no overlap in the reconciliation, promotion chain, or cost allocation logic.
Risk scorer parity repair involves replicating a black-box ML scorer's behavior, not reconciling cost centers or promotion chains for release artifacts.
Fixing a SQL report for cumulative sums and ranking is a pure SQL/window-function problem with no overlap in the multi-stage promotion chain or cost-center reconciliation logic.

Both tasks involve fixing a Python+SQLite reconciliation tool where the core bugs include deduplication (most-recent event wins), correct matching logic (cost center vs. charge-refund pairing), and idempotent ingestion—the central ideas and required fixes are essentially the same even though the domain names differ.
